---
title: "Project Topics"
subtitle: "16 suggested directions — or bring your own"
---

Every topic below is feasible on **free Colab** with datasets that download cleanly
(that was a selection criterion — Week 1's licensing lesson applies to projects too).
Difficulty: ⚙ solid (well-trodden, success is likely, rigor is the challenge) ·
⚙⚙ ambitious (a real design decision or two) · ⚙⚙⚙ adventurous (research-adjacent;
we help you scope it). Teams may also propose their own topic in this style.

Where a topic touches material we have not reached yet (GNNs, Weeks 6–13), the labs
will catch up with you before the proposal is due — planning around the syllabus is
part of the exercise.

## Track A · Node & graph prediction

**A1 · Beat the ladder on ogbn-arxiv** ⚙
Node classification on OGB's 170k-paper citation graph, with the course's honest
ladder as your baseline suite: structural statistics → community one-hots → DeepWalk
→ GCN/SAGE. *Dataset:* `ogb` (`ogbn-arxiv`). *Interesting because:* the OGB
leaderboard forces standardized splits, and the deliverable is a clean ablation of
*where* each accuracy point comes from — features, structure, or depth.

**A2 · Heterophily: when neighbors mislead** ⚙⚙
Weeks 1 and 3 kept warning about heterophilous graphs. Measure it: compare GCN-style
models against structure-blind MLPs and heterophily-aware variants on the classic
heterophilous benchmarks. *Dataset:* PyG's `WikipediaNetwork` (chameleon, squirrel) +
`Actor`. *Interesting because:* the field's own benchmarks here were criticized as
flawed — reproducing *that* critique is a legitimate angle.

**A3 · Molecular property prediction, honestly scaffolded** ⚙⚙
Graph-level prediction on `ogbg-molhiv` (or QM9 regression targets), with scaffold
splits versus random splits as the central experiment. *Dataset:* `ogb` /
PyG `QM9`. *Interesting because:* the random-vs-scaffold gap is the
pharma version of our leakage lessons — quantify it, explain it, and report which
model degrades most gracefully.

**A4 · Fraud detection on Elliptic** ⚙⚙
Classify illicit Bitcoin transactions on a real 200k-node temporal graph with heavy
class imbalance and a temporal split. *Dataset:* PyG `EllipticBitcoinDataset`.
*Interesting because:* it is heterophilous, imbalanced, and time-split all at once —
every honest-evaluation reflex from the course gets exercised, and PR-AUC (not
accuracy) is the story.

## Track B · Links, recommendations, time

**B1 · Link prediction three ways on ogbl-collab** ⚙
Heuristics (common neighbors, Adamic–Adar) vs shallow embeddings vs a GNN on a
collaboration graph with a *time-based* split. *Dataset:* `ogb` (`ogbl-collab`).
*Interesting because:* the heuristics are embarrassingly strong — explaining *when*
learning helps over counting is the actual contribution.

**B2 · A recommender from scratch on MovieLens** ⚙⚙
Bipartite user–item graph; implement BPR-style embedding factorization, then a graph
propagation model (LightGCN-style), evaluated with sane negative sampling and
Recall@K. *Dataset:* MovieLens-100k/1M — download directly from GroupLens (its
license permits research use; do not redistribute). *Interesting because:*
recommender evaluation is a minefield of leaks (popularity bias, sampled metrics) —
Week 3's and 4's pitfalls, at industrial scale.

**B3 · Temporal graph learning on TGB** ⚙⚙⚙
Pick one small TGB link-prediction task and compare a static-graph baseline
(retrained per snapshot) against a temporal method. *Dataset:* `py-tgb`
(`tgbl-wiki` is the small one). *Interesting because:* "does time actually help, or
is recency a sufficient feature?" has a measurable, frequently surprising answer.

**B4 · Relational databases as graphs (RelBench)** ⚙⚙⚙
Take one RelBench task and compare the graph-ML route against a strong tabular
baseline (gradient boosting on joined features). *Dataset:* `relbench` (pick a small
task). *Interesting because:* this is the newest frontier of "graphs in production"
(Week 14's topic) and the tabular baseline is genuinely hard to beat — either
outcome is publishable-grade insight for a course report.

## Track C · Knowledge graphs

**C1 · The pattern audit, at scale** ⚙
Week 4's cheat sheet as an empirical study: measure symmetry, inversion,
composition, and 1-to-N-ness per relation on FB15k-237 and WN18RR, then test whether
the measurements predict per-relation performance of TransE/DistMult/ComplEx/RotatE.
*Dataset:* PyG `FB15k_237`, `WordNet18RR`. *Interesting because:* it turns the
course's central KG theory into falsifiable predictions — Lab 4's showdown, in the
wild.

**C2 · KG completion on CoDEx** ⚙⚙
A cleaner, harder Wikidata-based benchmark with verified *hard negatives*. Train two
scorers, evaluate with the triple-classification task its negatives enable (not just
ranking). *Dataset:* CoDEx (github.com/tsafavi/codex, plain TSV files).
*Interesting because:* real labeled negatives — the thing Week 4 said KGs never give
you — exist here, and they change what you can honestly claim.

**C3 · Biomedical link prediction on ogbl-biokg** ⚙⚙
Drug–protein–disease completion (the hero example of Week 5, for real). Per-relation
evaluation, stratified by entity frequency (Pitfall 5). *Dataset:* `ogb`
(`ogbl-biokg`). *Interesting because:* the popularity-vs-truth failure mode is vivid
in biomedicine, and the stratified analysis is the contribution.

**C4 · Multi-hop queries: measure the easy/hard gap** ⚙⚙⚙
Implement Query2box-lite (Lab 5 gives you the skeleton), generate 2-hop and
intersection queries on FB15k-237, and produce the definitive easy-vs-hard-answer
analysis of Week 5 §3 — including how the gap changes with training epochs and
embedding dimension. *Interesting because:* you will produce the plot every
reasoning paper should contain and most don't.

## Track D · KGs meet LLMs

**D1 · GraphRAG vs vector RAG, refereed properly** ⚙⚙
Build both pipelines over a corpus you assemble (e.g., 50–100 Wikipedia articles on
one domain), with a question set stratified as in Week 5: single-fact, multi-hop,
corpus-global, fuzzy. Metric: supporting-fact coverage (Lab 5's), plus answer
correctness with a small local model or manual grading. *Interesting because:* the
honest routed comparison — which question types go to which retriever — is more
useful than either side's marketing.

**D2 · LLM-assisted KG construction, with a precision budget** ⚙⚙
Extract a KG from a document set with an LLM (local or API), then engineer the Week 5
repair pipeline: canonicalization, schema type-checking, provenance. Deliverable: an
extraction-precision study (sampled, hand-verified) before and after each repair.
*Interesting because:* everyone demos extraction; almost nobody measures it. The
measurement is the project.

**D3 · Can an LLM traverse?** ⚙⚙⚙
Give a language model the Week 5 toy KGs (serialized as triples in context) and
benchmark it on multi-hop conjunctive queries against Query2box and plain traversal,
as query depth and graph size grow. *Interesting because:* the failure curve of
in-context graph reasoning is a live research question you can chart with a small,
clean experiment.

## Track E · Reproducibility studies

**E1 · Reproduce a course paper's core claim** ⚙⚙
Pick one: node2vec's p/q effects (Fig. 3 of the paper), RotatE's phase histograms,
GCN vs the simplified SGC, or the FB15k leakage finding. Reproduce the central
figure/table from scratch, document every place the paper underspecified something,
and report where your numbers land. *Interesting because:* reproduction with a
discrepancy log is real science, teaches more than novelty, and the course's rigor
rubric rewards it fully.

**E2 · The tie-breaking audit** ⚙
Re-implement the ACL 2020 re-evaluation protocol: take two public KG-embedding
implementations, measure their score-tie rates, and quantify how much MRR moves
under optimistic vs random tie-breaking. *Dataset:* FB15k-237/WN18RR.
*Interesting because:* it is a small, sharp, fully-scoped project with a guaranteed
honest deliverable — ideal for a team that wants depth over breadth.

---

**Choosing:** pick the track that matches the weeks you enjoyed; check the dataset
downloads *this week*; and bring the proposal's "main risk" honestly — the best
proposals name the experiment that could kill the idea and schedule it first.
